title: Governor of South Carolina

context.text: This is an open seat: Republican Gov. Henry McMaster is ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

In the June 9 Republican primary, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette finished first but did not win a majority, triggering a June 23 runoff. Attorney General Alan Wilson won the runoff with 68.6% of the vote after President Trump announced support for both finalists.
Democratic state Rep. Jermaine Johnson won the June 9 Democratic primary with 59.7% of the vote over Billy Webster (29.6%) and Mullins McLeod (10.7%).

The Green Party's Walid Hakim and the United Citizens Party's Michael Addison, nominated at their parties' conventions, are also on the ballot, making four governor tickets in all. The State Election Commission's candidate-tracking list shows exactly these four tickets as active.

candidates.name: Alan Wilson
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate Mike Reichenbach, a state senator from Florence County. Won the June 23 Republican runoff with 68.6%.

summary.text: Alan Wilson has been South Carolina's Attorney General since 2011, elected in 2010 and re-elected three times. He won the Republican runoff for governor and is running with state Sen. Mike Reichenbach. His platform calls for eliminating the state income tax, government audits and expanded technical education, and he says he will continue defending the state's heartbeat abortion law.

background.text: Born in West Columbia, S.C.; earned a bachelor's degree from Francis Marion University (1996) and a law degree from the University of South Carolina School of Law (2002).
Colonel in the South Carolina National Guard's Judge Advocate General Corps; previously worked as an assistant solicitor and assistant attorney general.
First elected Attorney General in 2010 and re-elected three times, most recently in 2022.

priorities.text: Eliminating the state income tax, saying the state has a spending problem rather than a revenue problem.
priorities.quote: It's not a revenue problem. It's a spending problem.

priorities.text: Expanding technical and trade education pipelines that begin in high school.
Auditing state agencies, with Reichenbach leading the effort, and what the ticket describes as a law-and-order approach to public safety.

positions.summary: Said he has always supported defending South Carolina's Heartbeat Law, with exceptions, and his team confirmed he believes the six-week law should stand; he and Johnson both pledged at an October 6 debate not to seek to make the restrictions more severe.
positions.quote: What I have always supported is defense of South Carolina's Heartbeat Bill, obviously with exceptions.

positions.summary: As Attorney General he joined 27 other attorneys general in amicus briefs asking the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold state laws limiting girls' sports teams to biological females, and described the Court's June 2026 ruling as a landmark.
At the October 6 debate he said he wants every family to have access to health care but that expanding Medicaid is not the answer, arguing the state cannot afford it.

record.text: Announced that he joined 27 other attorneys general in friend-of-the-court briefs asking the U.S. Supreme Court to allow states to limit girls' sports teams to biological females, in cases from West Virginia and Idaho.
Issued a statement after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states can keep men out of women's school sports, noting he had joined a multistate amicus brief in the case.
As Attorney General, has defended South Carolina's abortion restrictions, including the 2023 Heartbeat law, in court.

candidates.name: Jermaine Johnson
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate Sam Skardon, former chair of the Charleston County Democratic Party. Won the June 9 Democratic primary with 59.7%.

summary.text: Jermaine Johnson is a state representative, former professional basketball player and small business owner who has served in the South Carolina House since December 2020. He is the Democratic nominee for governor, running with Sam Skardon. He supports expanding Medicaid, has opposed Republican-backed abortion laws and introduced a resolution calling for a moratorium on data centers.

background.text: Born in Los Angeles; earned a bachelor's degree from the College of Charleston, a master's from Strayer University and a doctorate in business administration from Northcentral University; played professional basketball from 2009 to 2015.
Took office in the South Carolina House in December 2020 and now represents District 52 (previously Districts 80 and 70). Serves on the House Labor, Commerce and Industry Committee.
His campaign says his accomplishments in office include expanding broadband access, repairing roads and bridges and creating the Lower Richland Tech Academy.

priorities.text: A change in leadership, arguing that voters are frustrated that their lives are not improving.
priorities.quote: If we elect the same type of leadership, we will get the same type of result.

priorities.text: Expanding Medicaid, which he called a must for improving access to health care.
A moratorium on data centers in South Carolina; his April 2026 resolution never received a vote.

positions.summary: Has opposed all Republican-backed anti-abortion laws in the Legislature, according to the SC Daily Gazette; at the October 6 debate he and Wilson both pledged they would not seek to make the state's abortion restrictions more restrictive.
Said at the October 6 debate that expanding Medicaid is a must for improving access to health care.

record.text: Introduced a resolution in April 2026 calling for a moratorium on all data centers in South Carolina; it did not receive a vote.
Co-sponsored 2023 legislation with Rep. Brandon Cox to place a monument honoring Robert Smalls on the State House grounds.

candidates.name: Walid Hakim
candidates.ballotNote: South Carolina Green Party nominee, running with Arnold E. Karr; nominated at the party's convention.

summary.text: Walid Hakim is the South Carolina Green Party's nominee for governor, running with Arnold E. Karr. He is a veteran, and was the party's nominee chosen at its convention.

priorities.text: A 100 Year Plan for South Carolina: sustainable infrastructure, state education and protecting remaining forests.
Health insurance for all residents through a state-owned nonprofit insurer.
Housing and economic reform, including a state-owned nonprofit bank and a cap of 12 residential properties per owner.

positions.summary: Lists full support for a woman's right to choose, including access to abortion, in his 10-point plan.
positions.quote: Full support for a woman’s right to choose, including access to abortion.

positions.summary: Proposes background checks, mental health screenings and required safety training for new gun owners, and says he has no intention of confiscating guns or implementing additional restrictions beyond those in place.
positions.quote: Smart Gun Safety Policy centered on secure background checks, mental health screenings, and required firearm safety training for all new gun owners.

positions.summary: Says he would support a progressive tax system.
positions.quote: support a progressive tax system where those who earn more contribute more, easing the burden on working and middle-class families.

positions.summary: Proposes state-funded childcare at every public school.
positions.quote: State-funded childcare at all schools to support working families.

positions.summary: Proposes a state-owned nonprofit insurer for all residents and accepting available federal Medicaid funds.
positions.quote: a state-owned insurer, offering full coverage to every resident

statements.quote: Reject cooperation with abuses by ICE; uphold the values of “The New Colossus.”
statements.context: On his campaign website, under 'LGBTQ+, Minority, and Immigrant Rights'

candidates.name: Michael Addison
candidates.ballotNote: United Citizens Party nominee, running with Candace Brewer, an activist.

summary.text: Michael Addison is the United Citizens Party nominee for governor, running with Candace Brewer. He was the Democratic candidate for South Carolina's 6th Congressional District in 2022.

priorities.text: Making South Carolina a state where people can afford to live, obtain healthcare and build a secure future.
An affordability agenda combining tax reform, better wages, affordable housing and Medicaid expansion.
Expanding access to care through a 'Palmetto Public Option' using telehealth.

positions.summary: Says he supports expanding Medicaid in South Carolina.
positions.quote: Yes. I support expanding Medicaid in South Carolina.

positions.summary: Says he supports raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour.
positions.quote: raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour

positions.summary: Proposes eliminating the state income tax with a sales-tax increase, and removing corporate sales-tax exemptions.
positions.quote: Corporations are exempt from sales tax, and we want to eliminate that loophole.

statements.quote: more affordable housing through rehabilitation of existing properties, workforce-housing partnerships, and more efficient permitting without sacrificing safety
statements.context: In responses to the Fort Mill Sun candidate questionnaire

researchNotes: Running mates are noted in each candidate's ballotNote rather than as separate entries. Ballotpedia was not reachable (it blocks automated requests) and the four-candidate slate was checked against the State Election Commission's Candidate Tracking System for the 11/3/2026 general election, which lists Wilson/Reichenbach (Republican), Johnson/Skardon (Democratic), Hakim/Karr (Green) and Addison/Brewer (United Citizens) as active; the SC Daily Gazette voter guide and The Green Papers agree. The repository has no South Carolina House roll-call snapshot, so no floor votes are cited for Rep. Johnson, and the official legislature page for his data-center resolution was not found (it is cited through SC Daily Gazette). Wilson's statement that he believes the six-week law should stand was relayed through his team after the debate, per the Gazette. Walid Hakim and Michael Addison were minimal entries; see the update at the end of these notes. Update: Hakim's positions come from the Policy Platform page of his campaign site (walidnhakim.com), and Addison's from the Fort Mill Sun candidate questionnaire (Oct. 14) and a WCSC interview (Sept. 24); both are now 'basic'. Addison's campaign site (addisonforsc.com) lists no issue positions.
